lead: Aurora grew fast in the 1970s to 1990s, and many of those homes now have aging pipes and roofs. Hail, basement leaks and freeze damage cause most water damage here.
risk: aging 1970s to 1990s plumbing, hail damage and frozen pipes
why: The median Aurora home was built in 1985, and many neighborhoods like Hoffman Heights, Village East and Mission Viejo went up in the decades around it. Some homes from the late 1970s to the mid-1990s have gray polybutylene supply pipe, which can crack at the fittings with age. Water heaters, washer hoses and original shutoff valves are now well past their expected life in many of these houses.

Aurora sits on the plains east of Denver, in the path of strong summer storms. Hail cracks shingles, dents siding and breaks windows, and leaks show up in the next rain. Winter brings fast swings, with mild days followed by hard freezes. Pipes in garages, crawl spaces and outside walls can split, and many homes have basements where the water ends up.

problems: 1980s homes in Village East, Mission Viejo
Homes with older sump pits and window wells
tips: Have a plumber check for gray polybutylene pipe.
Replace washer hoses and old shutoff valves.
Get the roof checked after any hail, even with no leak yet.
Disconnect garden hoses before the first freeze.
areas: Calls come from Original Aurora, Saddle Rock, Southlands, Tallyn's Reach, Hoffman Heights, Village East, Murphy Creek and Mission Viejo, plus Centennial, Parker and Denver.

faq.q: How do I know if my Aurora home has polybutylene pipe?
faq.a: Polybutylene is usually gray plastic pipe, sometimes with copper or plastic crimp rings. Look near the water heater, under sinks and where the line enters the house. It was common in homes built from about 1978 to 1995. Many insurers ask about it, and replacing it avoids a sudden failure.
